messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Anh's Burden

Anh Tran was twenty-two when he came to his first appointment, though his eyes held the weight of someone much older. He had been a relief worker in eastern Myanmar for fourteen months—part of a humanitarian organization providing medical aid in conflict zones—before the incident that changed everything. In March of last year, the clinic where he was working had been caught in crossfire between military forces and armed opposition groups. Anh had been helping evacuate patients when gunfire erupted through the building's walls. A colleague beside him was killed instantly. Anh survived by pressing himself into a concrete corner, unable to move, unable to help, listening to the screaming and the percussion of automatic weapons for what felt like hours but was probably thirty minutes. When soldiers finally secured the area, they moved through the clinic with rifles raised, checking bodies, checking rooms. One officer had stopped directly in front of Anh's hiding place, weapon trained at chest height, before lowering it and moving on. Anh had not moved for another hour after that, even after the shooting stopped. The silence, he would later say, was worse than the noise.

He returned to the United States two weeks later, telling his parents he was fine, that he needed to finish his degree. For the first month, he managed to attend classes at the university, though he found himself sitting at the back of lecture halls, always with an exit in sight. Then, in April, campus security had come into his biology lecture to do a routine presentation on safety protocols. The moment Anh saw the officer's uniform—the dark blue shirt, the belt heavy with equipment—his chest had seized. His hands had begun to shake uncontrollably. He had left the lecture hall without explanation and had not returned. The sight of that uniform had triggered something primal in him: a flooding sense of exposure and danger, and with it, an urgent conviction that he needed to disappear, to make himself small and invisible. From that day forward, he began to avoid anywhere he might encounter uniformed personnel. He stopped going to campus security events, took routes around the police station near his apartment, and started crossing the street whenever he saw someone in a military or law enforcement uniform approaching.

But avoidance had metastasized. Anh had come to believe that if he was being watched—if someone's eyes were on him—then something terrible was about to happen. The feeling of being observed had become synonymous with imminent threat. When classmates looked at him, when strangers glanced his way in the library, when he caught someone's eye in passing, his nervous system would surge with the same alarm it had known in that clinic. He began avoiding eye contact obsessively, training his gaze downward, angling his body away from others. He stopped attending social gatherings where friends from before the trauma might be present. His roommate had invited him to a house party in May; Anh had made an excuse and stayed in his room instead. The thought of seeing people who had known him before—people who might look at him, might expect him to be the same person he had been—felt unbearable. If they saw him now, if they really looked at him, they would see what he had become: someone who had failed at the one thing that mattered most.

That failure haunted him in a way that seemed to deepen with each passing week. Anh had gone to Myanmar with a clear sense of purpose—he was going to help, to save lives, to matter. Instead, he had hidden in a corner while people died. He had been paralyzed. His body had betrayed him then, and it continued to betray him now. Even in his apartment, even in complete safety, his heart would race without warning. His shoulders would tense. He would wake in the night drenched in sweat, convinced he could hear gunfire. His own physiology had become an enemy, a traitor that refused to acknowledge that the danger had passed. He was certain now that he could not trust his own body to keep him safe, that it would keep reacting as if he were still in that clinic, and there was nothing he could do to stop it. This sense of helplessness—the conviction that bad things would happen and he was powerless to prevent them—had begun to color everything. When he saw a police car, his mind immediately generated a cascade of catastrophic possibilities. When he felt someone's gaze on him, he was certain it preceded some form of harm. The triggers and the appraisals had become inseparable, each one feeding the other in a tightening spiral.

By the time Anh came to the clinic in late September, he had withdrawn almost entirely. He attended only essential classes, always alone, always vigilant. He had not seen his parents in three months despite living only forty minutes away—the thought of their concerned faces, their questions, their inevitable attempts to help him be "normal," felt impossible to face. He had lost twelve pounds. His GPA, once a source of quiet pride, had dropped from 3.8 to 2.9. What frightened him most was not the memories themselves, though those were vivid and intrusive, but the sense that he had become permanently broken—that the person he was before Myanmar was gone, replaced by someone who could not be watched, could not be around others, could not trust his own body, and could not stop the bad things from happening. He had finally called the university counseling center only because his mother had threatened to come to campus herself, and he could not bear the thought of her seeing what he had become.
